A depression, on the other hand, has no official cutoff number or textbook threshold at all. It is simply a recession that cuts much deeper and drags on for years. That is why an old joke from the 1950s, first recorded in print from Teamsters union president Dave Beck in 1954, popularized by former president Harry Truman in 1958, and reused by Ronald Reagan on the 1980 campaign trail, says that a recession is when your neighbour loses his job, and a depression is when you lose yours.

## How each word started as the softer one

The reason there is no neat boundary between a recession and a depression is that neither term began as a strict measurement. Each one started out as a softer word meant to avoid scaring the public.

Throughout the 1800s and early 1900s, severe financial crashes were called panics, such as the Panic of 1873 or the Panic of 1907, because depositors literally panicked and ran to pull their money out of the banks. Politicians disliked the word panic because using it only created more fear. When the stock market crashed in 1929, President Herbert Hoover and other officials leaned on a calmer-sounding word that had been used on and off since President James Monroe's time for a period of sluggish trade: a depression.

As the 1930s dragged on, the word depression stopped sounding calm and became the most frightening word in politics. When the economy finally began recovering and then tumbled again in 1937 and 1938, nobody in Washington wanted to tell voters they were sliding back into a depression. Instead, a milder word that economist Wesley Clair Mitchell had used in technical business-cycle research took over in everyday language for an ordinary downturn: a recession, just a temporary step back.

Seventy years later, that same habit gave the 2008 financial crisis its name. Calling the downturn of 2007 to 2009 the Great Recession was a way to say in two words that it was the worst economic slump since the 1930s, while still making clear that it never reached the scale of the Great Depression.

title: Bonds explained
summary: A bond is simply a loan sliced into small pieces so ordinary investors can lend money to a company or government in return for steady interest.
youtubeTitle: Bonds explained: why a bond is just a loan
body:
When a company or a government needs to borrow a lot of money, say to build a new factory or a highway, it doesn't have to walk into a bank and ask for a single giant loan. Instead, it can slice that big loan into thousands of small pieces and borrow the money straight from ordinary investors. Each of those pieces is called a **bond**, so when you buy a bond, all you're really doing is lending your money to the company or the government that issued it.

## How the payments work: coupon and maturity

Say you buy a ten-year bond from a company for $1,000 that pays 4 percent interest a year. Buying that bond means you've lent the company $1,000 upfront, and in return they promise to make two sets of payments to you over the life of the loan:

- **The coupon:** Every year for ten years, the company pays you 4 percent of your $1,000 loan, which comes out to $40 a year. In bond language, that regular annual interest payment is called the **coupon**.
- **Maturity:** When the ten years are up, at what's called **maturity**, the loan comes due and the company pays you back your full $1,000 principal.

Over the whole ten years, you collect ten yearly payments of $40 — $400 in interest in total — plus your original $1,000 back at the end.

## How a bond differs from a stock

Being a lender makes owning a bond very different from owning a **stock**. When you buy a stock, you become a part-owner of the company, which means your return is tied directly to how the business performs. If the company takes off and doubles in value, your stock goes up with it, and if the business does badly, your stock falls.

With a bond, you're not an owner at all — you're a **lender**. Even if the company becomes ten times bigger over the next decade, you don't share in that upside; you still only get your $40 a year and your $1,000 back at maturity.

On the other hand, the company has a legal obligation to pay you that interest whether it had a great year or a terrible one. And if the company ever goes bust, **bondholders are first in line** for whatever money is left over from selling off the business, before shareholders get a single cent.

## Why some bonds pay more than others

Being first in line doesn't make a bond risk-free, because if a bankrupt company doesn't have enough left over to cover its debts, bondholders can still lose their money. So just like with any other loan, the interest rate a bond pays depends on how safe the borrower is.

When you lend to the US government by buying a **Treasury bond**, you're almost guaranteed to get your money back, so the government only has to pay a few percent a year — around 4 percent on a ten-year Treasury — to find willing lenders. When you lend to a shaky company that might go bankrupt before the ten years are up, it has to offer a much higher interest rate, sometimes 8 or 10 percent a year on what people call a **junk bond**, just to convince anyone to take the risk. Whether a bond pays a little or a lot, though, the deal behind it is always the same: you're the lender, you collect steady interest along the way, and as long as the borrower holds up, you get your loan back at the end.
